carb-002.title: La Serre marks the start of the Carboniferous
carb-002.text: A rock face at La Serre, in the Montagne Noire of southern France, marks where the Carboniferous begins. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Siphonodella sulcata, descended from S. praesulcata. The marker has a flaw. Later study found S. sulcata below the boundary, weakening it.

carb-004.title: Crown tetrapods split and walk ashore
carb-004.text: Every living four-limbed animal descends from one of two lines that had already parted by the very start of the Carboniferous. Stem tetrapods had split into two crown lines: one leading to modern amphibians, the other to amniotes. The earliest confirmed land-dwelling tetrapods come from early Carboniferous deposits, some 20 million years after the first Devonian forms. Along the way, lineages with extra digits died out, which is why hands and feet carry no more than five. The survivors radiated on dry land and became the dominant land animals of the Carboniferous and Permian.

carb-012.title: Romer's gap, a hole in the tetrapod record
carb-012.text: For a stretch from the Tournaisian into the early Visean, tetrapod fossils are strikingly scarce. Paleontologists call it Romer's gap. Land vertebrates were recovering from the Hangenberg extinction, and the ichthyostegalian forms gave way to temnospondyls and reptiliomorphs. New finds at Blue Beach, Nova Scotia, and in Scotland are filling the gap, showing stem tetrapods and amphibians diversifying rapidly.

carb-014.title: Tropical seas build the Carboniferous Limestone
carb-014.text: The Yorkshire Dales and the Mendips were once warm tropical seabed. Shallow seas teeming with life laid down limestone widely across Britain and Ireland, in basins separated by landmasses such as the Wales-London-Brabant Massif. The rock is built from the shells and hard parts of corals, brachiopods and crinoids, set in carbonate mud. Later uplifted, it forms karst country, landscapes shaped by dissolving rock.

carb-003.title: Crinoids at their peak
carb-003.text: Near Clitheroe, England, some limestones consist almost entirely of crinoids, the stalked relatives of starfish. Camerate crinoids peaked in diversity in the Mississippian, and Agaricocrinus, about 345 million years old, was part of the radiation. From the Middle Mississippian their diversity fell, as shell-crushing fish and sharks multiplied.

carb-010.title: The last cladoxylopsid trees
carb-010.text: The cladoxylopsids built Earth's first forests in the Devonian. These large trees, ancestors of the ferns, and their order Pseudosporochnales lasted into the Early Carboniferous, and then they were gone.

carb-013.title: Sharks and ray-finned fish inherit the seas
carb-013.text: When the placoderms vanished, two groups moved into their place. After the end-Devonian Hangenberg extinction, sharks and their kin and ray-finned fish took over in diversity and abundance. Both had suffered too, since few Devonian species of either survived. Cartilaginous fish went through a major radiation, especially holocephalans such as the stethacanthids. The helicoprionids appeared, with a single circular whorl of teeth in the lower jaw. Around 350 million years ago, the first large sharks, ratfishes and hagfish appear.

carb-015.title: The Early Tournaisian Warm Interval
carb-015.text: A brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary did not last. The climate warmed again in the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval, 358–353 million years ago. The global average temperature was about 22 °C, with the tropics near 30 °C and the polar regions about 1.5 °C.

carb-016.title: Early Mississippian glaciations
carb-016.text: By about 350 million years ago, glacial layers were building up in the sub-Andean basins of Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay. A mid-Tournaisian glaciation left species-poor, frigid tundra in western Argentina. These short, minor glaciations came before the main ice age, steps in a gradual shift from greenhouse to icehouse.

carb-017.title: Temnospondyls begin the Age of Amphibians
carb-017.text: The first temnospondyls left their footprints before their bones. Their earliest traces are Tournaisian tracks, about 350 million years old; the first body fossils, such as Balanerpeton, are Visean, around 330 million years old. Often seen as primitive amphibians, temnospondyls flourished worldwide through the Carboniferous, Permian and Triassic. All their clades except one, the stereospondylomorphs, appeared during the Carboniferous. Their rise as the dominant land vertebrates earned the period the name Age of Amphibians.

carb-021.title: Lepidodendron, the scale tree
carb-021.text: Lepidodendron was a lycophyte, a relative of today's small clubmosses, but it grew into a massive tree. It first appeared near the Tournaisian–Visean boundary. With Sigillaria, it went on to dominate the coal swamps, with horsetails and seed ferns growing between them. Their order, the Lepidodendrales, lasted from the Carboniferous to the Late Permian.

carb-018.title: Aragonite seas replace calcite seas
carb-018.text: Seawater's chemistry decides what shells can be made of. From the early Carboniferous, the ratio of magnesium to calcium in seawater rose. By the Middle Mississippian, aragonite seas, which favor shells of the mineral aragonite, had replaced calcite seas. Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, followed in the Pennsylvanian.

carb-020.title: Insects take to the air
carb-020.text:
When did animals first take wing? The oldest known winged insects appear in the mid-Mississippian, though flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian.

Once airborne, they spread fast. Winged insects, the pterygotes, went through a major radiation across the Carboniferous, 358 to 299 million years ago. Sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids dominated at first, and cockroach relatives, the Blattoptera, became the most successful insects by the Pennsylvanian.

Two more innovations came in the Pennsylvanian. The Neoptera appeared. And the Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis, a life cycle with a separate larva, pupa and adult. Flight and metamorphosis together set up the insects for the success that followed.

carb-022.title: The Visean Warm Interval
carb-022.text: In the Visean Warm Interval, glaciers nearly vanished. They survived only in the proto-Andes of Bolivia and Argentina and in highlands of Brazil and southwest Africa, a pause before the ice returned in force.

carb-019.title: A long boom in marine life
carb-019.text: Some single-celled fusulinids grew so large that they hosted photosynthetic algae inside them. These foraminifera, with the brachiopods, led a long radiation of marine life, the Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event. It began in the Visean, with the main phase of the ice age. Fusulinids diversified extremely fast and peaked in the Visean, and so did bryozoans, renewed after the Hangenberg extinction. Cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined. The likely driver was geography. Closure of the Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, where species could evolve apart.

carb-023.title: East Kirkton's early land animals
carb-023.text: A Scottish quarry holds a crowd of early land animals. East Kirkton preserves land and freshwater life, and its richest layer dates to about 341 million years ago, in the Visean. It has yielded dozens of early tetrapods, including the temnospondyl Balanerpeton and the proto-amniote Westlothiana, nicknamed Lizzie, plus scorpions and eurypterids. Its mostly land-dwelling fauna reflects a wider Carboniferous move away from amphibious life.

carb-024.title: The Variscan collision at full strength
carb-024.text: Europe's Variscan mountains and North America's Alleghanian mountains were two parts of one continental collision. Gondwana and the terranes around it struck Laurussia obliquely, with metamorphism, igneous activity and large-scale deformation, and full collision came around 340 million years ago. Northwest Africa met southeastern Euramerica, raising the southern Appalachians and the Meseta and Mauritanide mountains. The main squeezing, the Sudetic phase, ran from about 330 to 320 million years ago, when Hercynian granites intruded central Europe. Together the two belts raised the Central Pangean Mountains, which reached their greatest height by about 295 million years ago.

carb-025.title: Pangaea comes together
carb-025.text:
Around 335 million years ago, the world's continents became one. Gondwana, Euramerica (Laurussia) and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea.

The assembly was not gentle. Plate motions sped up as the pieces converged, and the Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia closed. Pangaea was never truly finished, either: blocks kept joining and rifting away into the early Mesozoic. All told, it lasted about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 million years ago.

The supercontinent left its own proof. Glacial deposits of this age lie scattered from South America to Australia, on lands now oceans apart. Ice could not have spread across such distant places unless they were once joined, and those deposits later helped prove continental drift and the existence of Pangaea. The same collisions raised mountain belts such as {{ref:carb-024}} and set up the climates and ice ages of the following periods.

carb-026.title: The first reptiliomorphs
carb-026.text: The first reptiliomorphs, tetrapods on the line toward reptiles, appear between 335 and 325 million years ago. By the Visean, early tetrapods had radiated into at least three or four main branches. The reptile-like Westlothiana lived then.

carb-027.title: The ice age tightens its grip
carb-027.text:
Around 330 million years ago, an ice sheet kilometers thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole. It belonged to the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, which began between 335 and 330 million years ago, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and carbon dioxide fell.

The onset reshaped coastlines everywhere. Sea level fell worldwide, leaving unconformities, gaps in the rock record lasting millions of years. Ice spread from up to 30 centers across Gondwana. Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells, and the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian.

The ice left thick evidence. Its deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group. Those piles of scraped and dumped rock record ice that came and went for tens of millions of years.

carb-031.title: The Ouachita orogeny
carb-031.text: South America, then part of Gondwana, struck Laurussia's southern margin at an angle in the Ouachita orogeny. The collision began in the Late Mississippian. The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins, low areas in front of the range, such as the Delaware Basin. They fed rivers with sediment through the Pennsylvanian and Permian.

carb-032.title: The Serpukhovian extinction
carb-032.text: The worst extinction of the Carboniferous removed about 31% of marine genera in the early Serpukhovian. A major glaciation at the Visean–Serpukhovian boundary cooled the seas, picking off species adapted to narrow, tropical temperature ranges. Diverse crinoid and rugose-coral communities gave way to species-poor, cosmopolitan ones. Trilobites declined sharply while ammonoids peaked. It was driven more by a lack of new species than by high extinction, and its long-term ecological impact may have exceeded the end-Ordovician extinction's. It ties with the Hangenberg event as the seventh-worst post-Cambrian mass extinction. Its severity is debated: a 2026 study finds it weaker in North America, and sources dispute whether diversity afterward stagnated or surged.

carb-030.title: The Millstone Grit spreads over northern England
carb-030.text: The moors and rocky edges of the Pennines are made of old delta sand. With Britain near the equator, rivers from northern uplands and the Wales-Brabant High carried sand and mud into the Pennine Basin. When sea level fell as southern ice caps grew, deltas advanced across the region and left thick sandstones, the Millstone Grit. These gritstones lie beneath the Coal Measures.

carb-029.title: Avion's early insects
carb-029.text: Insects from the Avion locality in Pas-de-Calais, France, include the earliest known thrips and titanopterans.

carb-033.title: Amniotes and the egg that left the water
carb-033.text:
An egg that dries out is a dead egg. One tetrapod lineage solved that problem. It evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land, and these animals are the amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

When they arose is disputed. Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 million years ago, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 million years ago, while the Carboniferous article puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous. Clawed footprints from the Tournaisian of Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks. If so, amniotes go back to the start of the period or earlier. Researchers have not settled the question.

What is clearer is how they took over. Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes rose in their place.

carb-034.title: Patagonia meets Gondwana
carb-034.text: Igneous rocks 330–320 million years old under the North Patagonian Massif record subduction. It began in the early Carboniferous and lasted about 20 million years. The Patagonian landmass first touched Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous, and the broader collision came in the early Permian.

carb-036.title: Fossil Grove, a forest still standing
carb-036.text: In a Glasgow park, the stumps of an ancient forest still stand where they grew. About 325 million years ago, sediments buried tree-like lycopsids at Fossil Grove while they were upright. These Lepidodendron trees grew when Scotland lay in the tropics, near the equator.

carb-035.title: The Alleghanian orogeny builds the Appalachians
carb-035.text: Africa and North America collided in at least five separate deformation events. Africa was then part of Gondwana and North America part of Euramerica. The Alleghanian orogeny began about 325 million years ago and lasted some 65 million years, into the Permian. It built the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains, a wide, high chain along today's eastern seaboard, and helped form Pangaea. Sediment from the rising mountains filled basins such as the Black Warrior Basin. When West Africa struck in the Late Pennsylvanian, the compression turned northwest, and the same grinding raised the Little Atlas range around 300 million years ago.

carb-037.title: The Bear Gulch Limestone
carb-037.text: Central Montana's Bear Gulch Limestone preserves an unusually diverse fauna of cartilaginous fish, relatives of sharks, rays and chimaeras. Brachiopods, ray-finned fish and arthropods occur there too, along with Typhloesus, a puzzling animal that may be a mollusc.

openers.mississippian-subperiod: The Mississippian opens just after the Hangenberg extinction, with survivors moving in. Sharks and ray-finned fish took over the seas, and crinoids grew so thick that whole limestones are made of them. Stem tetrapods had already split into the lines leading to amphibians and amniotes, though their fossils are strangely scarce in a span called Romer's gap. Warm shallow seas laid down limestone across Britain and Ireland, but glaciers were building in South America. Seawater itself was changing, as aragonite seas replaced calcite seas.

reviews.mississippian-subperiod: The Mississippian joined the world together and then chilled it. Gondwana, Laurussia and Siberia came together as Pangaea, raising the Variscan, Ouachita and Alleghanian mountains and splitting the oceans into isolated regions where marine life boomed. As the main ice age took hold, sea level fell, the Serpukhovian extinction struck tropical species, and deltas spread the Millstone Grit. On land, tetrapods left Romer's gap behind: temnospondyls flourished, reptiliomorphs appeared, and amniotes, with eggs that survive on dry land, arose while insects took to the air.
